item.title: Shodoshima Olive Festival — Guide
item.description: Shodoshima, Japan’s olive island, celebrates its signature crop with olive-themed festivals and events, especially around the autumn harvest. Held at the Olive Park and around the island, these celebrations mark the harvest season with fresh olive tastings, new-season olive oil, olive-themed foods and sweets, craft stalls, music and the island’s sunny, Mediterranean atmosphere. It’s a chance to taste and buy the year’s produce, learn about olive cultivation, and enjoy the harvest spirit in the place where olives were first successfully grown in Japan.

item.title: Shodoshima Olives: Japan's Olive Island — Guide
item.description: Shodoshima, the second-largest island in the Seto Inland Sea, is Japan’s home of the olive. Its warm, dry, sunny climate proved ideal when olive cultivation was first successfully established here in the early twentieth century, and the island has embraced the crop ever since. Silvery olive groves cover the hillsides, and the Olive Park — with its Greek-style windmill, gardens and sea views — has a distinctly Mediterranean feel that draws visitors for photos and strolls.

item.title: Shodoshima Seaweed and Sea Produce — Guide
item.description: Shodoshima is famous for its olives, but the island’s food culture runs much deeper, rooted in the clean waters and mild climate of the Seto Inland Sea. Among its sea produce is wakame, the tender, nutritious seaweed harvested from the surrounding waters and used in miso soup, salads, and simmered dishes across Japanese cooking. Shodoshima also has a celebrated tradition of soy sauce brewing, with historic wooden-barrel breweries you can visit, and of tenobe somen, hand-stretched thin wheat noodles dried in the island air.

item.title: Kagawa Onsen Guide: Kotohira Hot Springs, Shodoshima Sea-View Baths, and City Rooftop Onsen
item.description: Kagawa is not a prefecture that advertises itself primarily as an onsen destination — it lacks the volcanic geology of Oita or the mountain-spring concentration of Nagano. But it has several genuinely excellent bathing options scattered across the prefecture, and the best of them are well-suited to the travel patterns of visitors who come for Konpira-san, Naoshima, and Sanuki udon. The Kotohira inn baths, the sea-view outdoor baths on Shodoshima Island, and the rooftop onsen hotels of Takamatsu are all capable of providing a memorable end to a cultural day in Shikoku.
